name: Adam and Eve, the Speke Hall Yews

location.address: Speke Hall, Speke Hall Avenue, Liverpool L24 1XD

access: National Trust property, paid entry (free to members). The courtyard is inside the house grounds; opening days are seasonal, check the National Trust before you go.
transport: Liverpool South Parkway and Hunts Cross stations are both about 2 miles (3 km) away, roughly 40 minutes on foot or a short taxi ride. Buses from the city centre reach South Parkway; there is no direct bus to the hall door.
story:
In 1712 the household at Speke Hall paid a man named Ezekiel Mason for making frames to set around the yew trees in the court. The yews are still there. Two of them fill the middle of the cobbled courtyard of this Tudor manor house on the southern edge of Liverpool, and they have names. Adam is the larger, a male tree measured at about 3.45 metres round in 2006. Eve, beside him, is female.

How old they are is a genuine disagreement. The Ancient Yew Group, which recorded the pair, says Adam's girth suggests something like 300 years, while noting that ring counts on pruned branches have been cited for much more. Wikipedia puts them at 500 years at least. So the honest band runs from roughly 300 to 500, and the one firm date is 1712, when the trees were already worth protecting.

They have had a famous visitor. Harriet Beecher Stowe came in 1853 and, in her travel book Sunny Memories of Foreign Lands, mentioned a single yew. A painting by James Campbell from the following year, now in the Walker Art Gallery, shows two large trees standing in the court, so the pair was certainly there by then.

The courtyard is inside the house grounds, which makes this a paid visit unless you are a National Trust member. The most recent record of the trees we can point to is the yew group's, so if you go, tell us how Adam and Eve are looking.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the two big yews in the middle of the cobbled courtyard, Adam the larger of the pair. They stand at the heart of Speke Hall, inside the house grounds.

name: The Eastham Yew

location.address: St Mary's Church, Church Lane, Eastham, Wirral CH62 0AB

access: Free. The church says the churchyard is open from light till night. The yew's base is railed off, so you see it from the path.
transport: In Eastham on the Wirral, outside Liverpool. Merseyrail Wirral line from Liverpool Central to Eastham Rake, roughly 25 to 30 minutes, then about 20 minutes on foot.
story:
The story told in Eastham is that when the abbot and monks of St Werburgh in Chester received the manor in 1152, the villagers asked them to look after the old yew. Old, in 1152. The tree still stands in St Mary's churchyard in Eastham, on the Wirral, and the church describes it as the oldest tree in Wirral.

How old is a matter of claims, and none of them is a measurement. A Royal Archaeological Society visit in 1898 said possibly 1,500 years, and suggested it was planted against the east end of a wattle-and-daub chapel from before the Norman Conquest. The church's website now says it is believed to be over 1,800 years. Nobody has dated it, so hold both figures as claims.

The measurable part is the trunk. The Ancient Yew Group recorded it in 1999 at 6.40 metres round at chest height and classes it as ancient.

It has not always been loved. A local history site says many people have tried to destroy it over the years, which is why it stands behind railings. Someone also hid a sword in its topmost branches. It was found some years ago and is displayed in the church.

Eastham is outside Liverpool, a day trip of about 50 minutes each way, by Merseyrail from Liverpool Central to Eastham Rake and then on foot.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the railings around its base, the one fenced-off yew in the churchyard, 6.4 metres round. It stands east-south-east of St Mary's church in Eastham, on the Wirral.
